subject: ela
cluster: Range of reading and level of text complexity
description: Students read and comprehend grade-appropriate literature (stories, dramas, and poems) within the grades 6 to 8 text complexity band and demonstrate understanding by answering questions about it. They track who is speaking and acting, follow the sequence and cause-and-effect of events, determine the meaning of unfamiliar words and figurative phrases from context, identify what the text states explicitly, draw reasonable inferences about character, setting, plot, mood, and theme, and summarize the central idea of a passage. This is an integrative comprehension skill: rather than isolating one strategy, each item asks the student to make sense of a complete literary excerpt at a level of complexity appropriate to sixth grade. Every item embeds the full passage or excerpt it depends on, so the student needs nothing external to answer.
subSkills: Identify the speaker, narrator, or characters and keep track of who does and says what
Follow the sequence of events and the cause-and-effect relationships among them
Determine the meaning of unfamiliar words and figurative phrases using context clues in the passage
Distinguish information stated explicitly from conclusions that must be inferred
Draw reasonable inferences about character traits, motives, setting, mood, and emerging theme
Summarize the central idea or gist of a literary passage without copying it word for word
Read texts across literary forms (prose narrative, drama, and poetry) and adjust to each form's conventions
Sustain comprehension across a longer, more complex passage at the upper end of the grade band

problemArchetypes.name: Comprehend explicit detail
problemArchetypes.example: Passage: 'By the time the bus reached the lake, the rain had stopped and the clouds were breaking apart. Priya pressed her face to the window, counting the sailboats already on the water.' Question: According to the passage, what had happened to the weather by the time the bus arrived? Answer: The rain had stopped and the clouds were breaking apart, because the text states this directly.

problemArchetypes.name: Determine word meaning from context
problemArchetypes.example: Passage: 'The trail grew so steep that the hikers had to clamber over the boulders, using both hands to haul themselves up.' Question: What does the word 'clamber' mean as it is used here? Answer: To climb with effort using hands and feet, because the passage describes using both hands to haul themselves up steep rocks.

problemArchetypes.name: Sequence and cause-and-effect
problemArchetypes.example: Passage: 'Daniel left the gate open when he ran inside for his glove. By the time he came back, the puppy was gone, and he spent the rest of the afternoon calling its name down the street.' Question: What caused the puppy to get loose? Answer: Daniel left the gate open when he ran inside, which let the puppy out.

problemArchetypes.name: Infer character or mood
problemArchetypes.example: Passage: 'Mara read the audition results twice. Then she folded the paper into a small square, slid it into her back pocket, and walked the long way home, past the empty theater.' Question: What can the reader most reasonably infer about how Mara feels? Answer: She is disappointed, because folding the results away, taking the long way home, and passing the empty theater suggest sadness even though the text never names the feeling.

problemArchetypes.name: Summarize the central idea
problemArchetypes.example: Passage: 'For three weeks Theo practiced the same eight measures until his fingers ached. He missed two birthday parties and a movie. On the night of the recital he played them without a single mistake, and the small ache in his hands felt like a fair trade.' Question: Which statement best summarizes the passage? Answer: Theo's steady practice and sacrifice paid off when he performed the piece perfectly, because the passage centers on effort leading to success.

problemArchetypes.name: Comprehend across literary form (poem or drama)
problemArchetypes.example: Poem: 'The old clock on the stair / forgets to keep the time, / yet every evening at six / it remembers how to chime.' Question: What does the poem suggest about the clock? Answer: The clock is unreliable for telling time but still chimes faithfully each evening, because it 'forgets to keep the time' yet 'remembers how to chime' at six.

Easy.description: A short literary stimulus of roughly 2 to 5 sentences (about 30 to 70 words) at the lower edge of the grade band, embedded in the item. The question targets information stated explicitly or a single context clue, and the answer can be located almost directly in the text. Vocabulary is mostly familiar and any figurative language is transparent. Minimal inference is required.
constraints: Stimulus is 2 to 5 sentences (about 30 to 70 words) included in the prompt
Targets an explicit detail, a clear sequence step, or one supported context-clue word
Identify-level task: locate the answer that the passage states or signals directly
Distractors are details from elsewhere in the passage or plainly off topic

Medium.description: A literary stimulus of roughly 6 to 10 sentences (about 80 to 130 words), such as a full narrative paragraph, a short scene of drama, or a brief poem, embedded in the item. The task requires a single-step inference (a character's feeling, motive, or trait, a cause-and-effect link, or the gist of the passage) or determining a less obvious word meaning from context. The student must connect details rather than copy one sentence, and distractors are real text details that are too narrow, partial, or off point.
constraints: Stimulus is a 6 to 10 sentence paragraph, short scene, or brief poem in the prompt
Targets a one-step inference, a cause-and-effect relationship, or a central-idea summary
Analyze-level task: combine two or more details to reach a supported conclusion
Distractors are genuine but weaker readings, partial summaries, or surface-only details

Hard.description: A richer literary stimulus of roughly 11 to 16 sentences (about 150 to 230 words) at the upper end of the grades 6 to 8 band, with more figurative, implicit, or layered content, embedded in the item. The task requires multi-step inference or evaluation: judging the best summary of a developing situation, inferring theme or a shift in a character across the passage, interpreting figurative language in context, or synthesizing several details into the central idea. The student must hold the whole passage in mind and weigh competing reasonable-sounding options.
constraints: Stimulus is an 11 to 16 sentence passage, full short scene, or complete poem in the prompt
Targets multi-step inference about theme, character development, or figurative meaning
Evaluate-level task: select the best overall summary or interpretation and reject close-but-wrong ones
Distractors include a true-but-too-narrow detail, an overstated or off-theme reading, and a literal misread of figurative language

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student treats a reasonable-sounding outside assumption as if the passage said it, answering from prior knowledge rather than the text
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Chooses a detail or motive that fits a familiar stereotype or what 'usually' happens but is never stated or supported in the passage

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student confuses a small supporting detail with the central idea and summarizes only one part of the passage
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Picks a summary that restates a single vivid sentence rather than the main point of the whole excerpt

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student reads figurative or descriptive language literally and so misunderstands what the passage means
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Reads 'the clock forgets to keep the time' as proof the clock is broken on the inside rather than as a way of saying it runs unreliably

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student guesses a word's meaning from how it looks or sounds instead of using the context clues in the passage
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Defines 'clamber' as 'to be loud' because it resembles 'clamor,' ignoring the surrounding description of climbing over boulders

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student reverses or confuses cause and effect, or mixes up the order of events
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Says the puppy ran away first and that is why the gate was open, reversing the actual cause-and-effect relationship

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student confuses an inference with something stated explicitly, treating a reader conclusion as a direct statement in the text
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Marks 'Mara is disappointed' as directly stated when the passage only describes her actions, from which the feeling must be inferred

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student overgeneralizes one detail into a sweeping theme the passage does not actually support
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Concludes the passage is about how practice never matters when the text shows practice leading to a successful performance
